analytic.title: Real-time task scheduling in a FaaS cloud

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Today, Function-as-a-Service is the most promising concept of serverless cloud computing. It makes possible for developers to focus on application development without any system management effort: FaaS ensures resource allocation, fast response time, schedulability, scalability, resiliency, and upgradability. Applications of 5G, IoT, and Industry 4.0 raise the idea to open cloud-edge computing infrastructures for time-critical applications too, i.e., there is a strong desire to pose real-time requirements for computing systems like FaaS. However, multinode systems make real-time scheduling significantly complex since guaranteeing real-time task execution is challenging even on one computing node with multi-core processors. In this paper, we present an analytical model and a heuristic partitioning scheduling algorithm for a partitioned scheduling system suitable for real-time FaaS platforms of multi-node clusters. We present the architecture of the envisioned real-time FaaS platform, emphasize its benefits and the requirements for the underlying network and nodes, and survey the related work that could meet these demands.
Index Terms-real-time scheduling, real-time cloud, real-time FaaS, partitioned scheduling, partitioned-EDF, heterogeneous multiprocessor, multi-node and multiprocessor system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the advent of 5G, IoT, and Industry 4.0, the idea of running delay-sensitive applications in the cloud instead of special-purpose hardware is gradually gaining ground. As [1] argues, cyber-physical systems, IoT, and cloud computing together create Industry 4.0, i.e., makes the concept of "smart factory" alive. This paves the way for use-cases that were considered impossible before, such as remote-controlled factories. Novel applications of Industry 4.0 require reliable wireless connections, ultra-low end-to-end latency, high data rates, and support for a massive number of devices. Fortunately, these characteristics are enabled by 5G [2], [3]. E.g., the authors of [4] present how 5G can facilitate a distributed robotics control system. They allow time-critical and computationally exhaustive operations to be offloaded to the cloud using 5G URLLC (Ultra-reliable low-latency communication) between the cloud and the robot. These technologies lead to the idea of opening up cloud and edge computing infrastructures for timecritical applications, such as cloud-assisted safety systems, tactile internet, virtual and augmented reality applications.

Thanks to its flexibility benefits, serverless computing has become one of the most popular paradigms in the field of cloud computing. It allows developers to focus only on application development and not care about the server management and auxiliary functions by providing resource alloca-tion, fast response time, schedulability, scalability, resiliency, and upgradability of the deployed applications. Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) -the best-known implementation of serverless computing -makes it possible for users to run their microservice applications without any management effort. Most of the FaaS platforms rely on container technologies, like LXC or Docker, and container orchestration systems such as Kubernetes. Typically, the users' source code is wrapped into containers that are scheduled and deployed by Kubernetes. Containerization provides isolation of processes and libraries with low-performance overhead.

Although several research initiatives have tackled the idea of running real-time (RT) applications in containers [5]- [7], it still seems to be an undiscovered research field today. This is especially true if both real-time and traditional containers are scheduled on the same hardware. E.g., for critical applications, characterized by deadline requirements, real-time containers could be an appropriate choice. Mixed-Criticality Systems (MCS) are able to handle such apps with various levels of criticality. They ensure the correct execution of critical tasks while enabling the sharing of the underlying hardware resources. In the beginning, such systems used single-core architecture machines, but later, MCS hardware with multicore architectures emerged. To our knowledge, currently, there is no solution that would be capable of scheduling RT tasks on a cluster of servers. No wonder, since such a cluster system has many requirements which are still actively researched: 1) underlying networks need to be deterministic, 2) the operating systems (or hypervisors) of the cluster's servers are required to be real-time, 3) it must support spatial and temporal real-time scheduling of tasks, 4) it has to take into account the heterogeneity of the computing infrastructure and its configuration.

In this paper, we introduce -to the best of our knowledge the first and only -real-time FaaS (RT-FaaS) system, which extends the current RT platforms by bringing in the distributed aspect. We collect the related technical requirements and research challenges essential for such an RT cloud computation system. In addition, we propose a possible real-time scheduling method for such a system to ensure the RT execution of user functions. Besides, by summarizing the real-time results published in different computer science fields, we aim to start a new research direction, called real-time FaaS, and encourage the research community to contribute.

The structure of the paper is the following. Sec. II presents the envisioned architecture of the RT-FaaS concept. Sec. III summarizes the related works. Sec. IV elaborates on the research problem and introduces the assumed environment models, we argue for partitioning scheduling in systems like RT-FaaS. Sec. V presents our proposed partition algorithm and we make its evaluation in Sec. VI. Sec. VII discusses the benefits of our algorithm, emphasizes the limitations of the assumed scheduling model, and presents our planned future works. Finally, Sec. VIII concludes the paper.

II. THE CONCEPT OF REAL-TIME FAAS Figure 1: The envisioned main components of RT-FaaS system By RT-FaaS, we mean a serverless computing system, where RT and non-RT functions can run together such that deadline requirements are met, while many of the well-known benefits of cloud architectures are still ensured. Such an envisioned platform is depicted in Fig. 1. This system performs both temporal and spatial scheduling of the incoming function deployment requests. It determines where -on which processor of the cluster -and when -in which time interval -to run functions to meet their deadline requirements if they have any. In RT-FaaS, users define their functions, and depending on whether it is an RT task or not, they also configure the maximum tolerated response time and period. The former determines the maximum time for the function's response to arrive back to the user's ingress point. The period defines the frequency of the function request. A practical example for such an RT function might be a video frame processing tool [8] that receives each snapshot image of a video stream, analyzes it, and returns the detections to the user. E.g., in the case of an 80 fps video stream, a new frame arrives at every 12 ms, which is the period of the video processing function.

The function deployment requests are submitted through the FaaS platform interface where the system collects them into a Function Set and initiates the deployment process. RT-FaaS manages a cluster of hosts (e.g., physical machines in a datacenter topology) including their processors (CPUs) and the underlying network. The ingress points are the interfaces where input and output of the deployed functions pass through and are connected to the internal network of the cluster. During a deployment process, the system must decide where and when to run the requested functions to fulfill the deadline requirements. We argue, more than one scheduler together could perform this task. The RT-FaaS Scheduler determines the functions' location inside the cluster (e.g., a target host or processor), while multiple OS-level schedulers decide when to run them. An OS-level scheduler might be associated to the host or to one of its processors.

As soon as a function is deployed, in each period through the ingress point, its input data reaches the target host where the function is ready to process it if the scheduler permits execution. The function might optionally call third-party cloud services like database writing and reading or messaging. Finally, when the function finishes, it sends its response back via the ingress point. We call this function request cycle the response time of the function, which formally is defined in Definition 1. The goal is to complete this function request cycle before the function's deadline.

div.head: Definition 1. Response time of a function:
div.p: The necessary time for i) the input data reaching the target host, ii) function being executed, iii) performing its third-party service calls, and iv) sending its response back to the ingress point.

Ideally, an RT-FaaS platform -and its underlying server infrastructure -operates on a deterministic network where the speed and latency of data transfer are guaranteed. Novel networking standards like Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) and Deterministic Networking (DetNet) [9]- [11] strive to bring this new level of determinism into the life of networks. It is also essential for operating systems of the infrastructure servers to work in real-time. I.e., they assure the applications get the required processor cycles to meet their deadlines.

As we mentioned earlier, RT scheduling of applications in both space and time is challenging. There are well-known single-core (e.g., Earliest Deadline First -EDF) and multicore (e.g., Global EDF -G-EDF) scheduling approaches [12], but unknown barriers may occur when controlling multiple processors of multiple nodes. Although at first this problem seems equivalent to the cluster scheduling problem [13], there are crucial differences in the details. We argue the global scheduling on multiple hosts is not feasible with the algorithms known today. They all assumes a single node architecture, containing multiple processors, where the ready state tasks are selected by the processors from the ready task queue. In contrast, in a multi-node system, each server contains its own ready task queue. If such a queue and a ready state processor are located on separate nodes, first the task need to be migrated from host A to host B, where the execution will be performed. The added task migration time between the hosts would slow down the cluster's computing performance to a level that makes the system unusable. Indeed, the scheduling overhead is on the order of micro-or milliseconds, as opposed to migrating tasks that would even take up to seconds.

The heterogeneity of available processors must also be taken into account, which can greatly affect the quality of scheduling. The processors used for scheduling are typically divided into three categories: identical, uniform heterogeneous, and unrelated heterogeneous processors. In identical multiprocessor platforms, all CPU processing speeds are the same. The uniform heterogeneous multiprocessor platforms contain CPUs with various processing speeds. Finally, in unrelated heterogeneous multiprocessor platforms, the processing speed depends on both the CPU speed and the function being executed. E.g., a GPU would execute graphics jobs faster than CPUs. Related to identical processors, several scheduling studies have already been published, but in our opinion, an unrelated heterogeneous processor set needs to be assumed for the case of future RT-FaaS systems. In this case, the runtime of the tasks depends on which processor they are running on. Such a situation can occur in many cases: i) the available servers forming the cluster for the RT-FaaS contains different types of processors, ii) the RT tasks read and writes externalized states whose access time affects the processing time of the task, and iii) RT tasks also could call future RT cloud services whose response time may depend on the host from where the service was called. E.g., such a service could be a low-latency RT cloud database, event streaming and messaging, or Artificial Intelligence (AI) model.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: Most of the challenges discussed in Sec. II are actively researched topics in academia. We summarize the current state of them in this section.

Deterministic Physical Networks: The underlying network of a RT-FaaS system should be deterministic. Such networks are highly reliable, providing bounded latency and low jitter. The two networking standards in this field are IEEE 802.1 TSN [9], and IETF DetNet [14] which provide deterministic and reliable packet forwarding for link-layer and networklayer services. The authors of [11] analyze the similarities and differences between them and give a survey of the published standards and possible future areas. [10] surveys the studies of TSN and DetNet that specifically target the support of Ultra-Low Latency (ULL) in 5G networks.

Deterministic Virtual Networks: However, not only the network must be latency bounded, but other communications within the server hosts as well. Gutiérrez et al. present a study [15] about the Linux communication stack meant for real-time robotic applications. They proved, under appropriate configuration, the Linux kernel -which is not optimized for bounded latencies -greatly enhances the deterministic nature of communications if there is no significant non-critical concurrent traffic in the system. If there is, they demonstrated how this can disrupt the bounded latencies. On the other hand, there exist network stacks with the specific purpose of providing deterministic networking. Such an approach is RTnet [16], an open-source hard real-time network protocol stack for Linux equipped with real-time extension RTAI or Xenomai. RTnet implements UDP/IP, TCP/IP, ICMP, and ARP in a deterministic way, and it is able to handle RT and non-RT traffic jointly.

Li et al. in [17] realize the Xen hypervisor handles RT and non-RT traffic through its common interface. They identify limitations that could result in long or unpredictable network traffic latencies between virtual machines (VMs). They propose VATC, a Virtualization-Aware Traffic Control framework to improve predictability and to reduce the delay for latency-sensitive applications. In [18], the authors of RT-Xen 2.0 present a new real-time multicore VM scheduling framework in the popular Xen virtual machine monitor. This enables real-time VM scheduling (both global and partitioned) in virtualized hosts. They also integrated their work into OpenStack for co-hosting real-time and regular VMs in [19].

Real-Time Containers: The demand for more lightweight solutions, which do not require a full-blown virtualization layer, has increased. Struhár et al. provide a systematic literature survey [5] that summarizes the research community's effort on bringing real-time properties to container-based virtualization. [6] provides a reference architecture scheme for implementing the RT container concept -allowing critical containers to cohabit with traditional, non-RT containers on the same hardware -on top of a Linux kernel patched with a hard real-time co-kernel. Abeni et al. [7] propose to use a real-time deadline-based scheduling policy built into the Linux kernel to provide temporal scheduling guarantees to different co-located containers. They implemented a hierarchical scheduling system such that it is compatible with the most commonly used container-based virtualization solutions.

Real-Time Serverless Platforms: Today's serverless computing platforms cannot provide invocation rate guarantee of deployed functions. They instead give best-effort service, making them unable to support bursty and real-time applications. However, the authors of [20] have tackled this issue and propose an extension to serverless, called real-time serverless, to guarantee the demanded invocation rate. They argue the application's ability to acquire compute resources depends on the function invocation latencies. If they lag the application requirements, the application will not get enough compute resources in time, resulting in the application not finishing before its deadline. The proposed design ensures the required invocations will be available, thus providing enough computation power to execute the function before the deadline.

Real-Time CPU Scheduling: Suppose physical and virtual networks, the hypervisors, the containers, and VMs themselves all provide real-time services. In that case, the remaining essential criteria is to make the hosts' operating system (OS) real-time too, i.e., apply RT task scheduling. When only a single processor exists, the mandatory scheduling solution to read is Liu and Layland's study [21] about EDF. If multiple processors exist, the proposed multiprocessor scheduling approaches can be divided into two categories: partitioned and global techniques. The former uses a partitioning method to spread the tasks onto processors and run a mono-processor scheduling algorithm (e.g., EDF) on each core. This is a static scheduling approach, i.e., the task migration between the cores is not allowed. On the other hand, global scheduling is a dynamic approach that has a single global scheduler that determines when and on which core to run the task. Here task migration is allowed, i.e., each task could run on each processor at any time.

Several results have been published for partitioned scheduling of RT tasks on multicore systems. However, these works are generally tailored for a single node environment, including multiple processors or cores. In contrast, we believe for RT-FaaS, multiple processors of multiple nodes are to be managed to execute both RT and non-RT tasks. Consequently, we argue that the known RT scheduling algorithms are not applicable to the envisioned RT-FaaS system.

Existing papers which study the partitioned scheduling problem of RT tasks typically consider either identical cores or processors as [22]- [24] or only a limited heterogeneity among of them (e.g., dual-core types of the ARM big.LITTLE architecture) [25]- [27]. [28], [29] propose methods running in non-polynomial time to solve the partitioning problem. Baruah in [30] presents the Heterogeneous Multiprocessor Partitioning Problem that is relatively similar to the one we assume for RT-FaaS (see in Sec. IV-D). The proposed approximation algorithm aims to minimize the maximum fraction of the capacity of any processor that is utilized to process RT tasks.

Global scheduling is also a highly investigated topic. E.g., [31] propose a new, more realistic model with a hierarchical platform view for global scheduling on unrelated processors and present several new workload assignment methods. We argue that RT task migration cannot be completed efficiently in a multi-node RT-FaaS system with the methods known today. Hence, in this paper, we focus our efforts on partitioned scheduling.

div.head: IV. RESEARCH PROBLEM: SCHEDULING IN RT-FAAS
div.p: In this section, we define the proposed research problem, i.e., how to schedule RT and non-RT functions, simultaneously, in an RT-FaaS such that deadlines are met and non-RT tasks are not starved. We assume a multi-node multiprocessor cloud computing system, i.e., a cluster of servers connected by a LAN, and managed by the RT-FaaS platform with the goal of scheduling the user demanded functions according to Definition 2.

div.head: Definition 2. The objective of the proposed RT-FaaS scheduler is to assign RT tasks to a minimum number of processors of the server cluster, such that the deadline requirements are met.
div.p: Although a processor may run both RT and non-RT tasks, as Brosky argues in [32]: a shielded CPU makes it possible to guarantee rapid response to external interrupts and to provide a more deterministic environment for executing realtime tasks. Indeed, Gutiérrez et al. in [15] demonstrate that although the communication delay, when the system is under heavy load, can be mitigated by using a real-time kernel, whenever there is concurrent traffic for non-RT tasks, it is not enough. They show that isolating the real-time application and the corresponding interrupt to a CPU can effectively avoid high latencies. The objective function in Definition 2 leaves as many processors as possible to process the remaining non-RT functions, thus, ensures that they will not starve for the CPU cycle.

In this paper, we consider a partitioned-EDF scheduling system for RT-FaaS and propose a partitioning algorithm that takes into account the heterogeneity of the processors and attempts to minimize the number of utilized CPUs for the RT tasks. We elaborate on the assumed environment and the partitioning problem to solve. In order to be able to focus on CPU scheduling, we make the following assumption: Assumption 1. We assume that RT-FaaS operates on a deterministic network both among the hosts and within the hosts between the Network Interface Controller (NIC) and the RT function.

We are aware of the fact that this is a significant constraint for the platform. However, as deterministic networking is an actively researched topic, we believe that this requirement will be increasingly met in the future.

div.head: A. Deployment and Function model
div.p: We have modeled the deployment that RT-FaaS users may request to deploy. The deployment process includes i) selecting the host and its processor where the container will be deployed to run the real-time function, ii) configuring the network between the ingress point of the RT-FaaS system and container, and iii) scheduling the function in a real-time manner. Definition 3. A deployment is modeled by three parameters (τ, R, T ), where τ is the function -i.e., the source code to run -R is the response time of the function -defined in Definition 1 -running in the RT-FaaS, and T is the trigger period of the function. In a multiprocessor system, parameter R is a set of response times for each processor.

In this paper, we consider implicit deadlines, which means each function's deadline equals its period. Assuming that hosts in the infrastructure contain heterogeneous multiprocessors, R includes multiple response times, one for each processor. If n deployment requests arrive simultaneously, the RT-FaaS system needs to schedule n functions on the managed host cluster and configure the network routes back and forth to the target server where functions are running. Please note that we use terms function and task interchangeably due to the fact that in FaaS terminology, the former is used while real-time scheduling terminology prefers the latter. Each deployment contains a function τ . To describe them, we have used the function model defined in Definition 4. The functions are assumed to be periodic tasks and each of them is defined by three parameters.

div.head: Definition 4. A function is determined by τ = (C, T, D),
div.p: where C is the worst-case execution time (WCET), T is the release period, and D is the deadline for the execution.

The tasks' utilization can be calculated by u = C D . Similarly to the deployment model, if hosts in the infrastructure contain heterogeneous multiprocessors, the parameter C and D are also a set of possible elements depending on the processor on which the task is processed.

div.head: B. Relations between deployment and function model
div.p: It is not realistic that users define all the parameters related both to the deployment and function models. Let us assume a deployment request which includes an object detection algorithm as a function. It detects objects on the input video stream's frames, writes the number of detected elements to a database (DB) -through a real-time cloud DB serviceand also returns this value. Most likely, in the best case, the user is able to define only i) the source code of the function, ii) the WCET c of this algorithm without any third party service call, iii) the frame rate of the input video stream, and iv) the RT cloud service used by the uploaded function. In this example, the frame rate of the input video is equivalent to the deployment period T , while the RT cloud service is the DB writing. In the following, we show how to determine the other required parameters from these.

The response time R of a deployment depends on the location and the performance of the processor which executes the deployment's task τ . Besides the function's execution, the RT-FaaS platform -due to the network delay among the hosts and the ingress point -needs to consider the transmission time of the task's input and output workload. Moreover, during the execution, it is also possible that it takes advantage of some RT cloud services (e.g., DB accesses). In such a case, the worst-case execution time of the task becomes C = ω(t RT service ) + c, where t RT service is the execution time of the applied RT cloud service -including the transmission times between the RT function and the RT cloud service -provided by the RT-FaaS, ω is the number of the RT cloud service calls, and c is the time needed to run the code of the function. The response time of a deployment shall be R = t i→f + C + t f →i , where t i→f and t f →i are the transmission times between the ingress point and the function. While c and ω are defined by the user, in a distributed system, both the transmission times and the real-time cloud service execution time may depend on the processor where the deployment's functions are running. Consequently, these transmission and execution times rely on the RT FaaS system scheduler, or more precisely, the partitioning of the requested functions. Note, in a real-world scenario, transmission times depend on the transmission channel condition, however, we neglect this effect (Assumption 1).

For an illustration of these parameter relations, let us examine Fig. 2. The axis shows the timeline of the previously mentioned use-case: the periodically triggered object detection function. We depict the function and the deployment-related parameters in red and green colors. This example assumes that the task performs one real-time service access during its execution. T tells us how frequently a new video frame arrives at the ingress point of the FaaS system, i.e., how frequently the deployment is triggered to process the frame. R is the response time for the trigger which is obtained by summing the network-related transmission times (t i→f , t f →i ) and the worst-case execution time C of the task. In the figure, we have divided C into two parts: one part c 1 before the real-time service call and one c 2 after that. Needless to say, though in this example, we have assumed only one service call, the function could use multiple services and access them more than once. We assume that the task reserves the processor during the external real-time DB access, i.e., the C = c 1 + c 2 + t RT service . The deadline for the task is the deadline for the deployment trigger's response time without the transmission times, i.e., D = Tt i→ft f →i . In this way, it is guaranteed that the processed task's return value has enough time to get back to the ingress point. As a result of Assumption 1, t i→f , t f →i , t RT service are all constants and the RT-FaaS platform is aware of their values.

div.head: C. Infrastructure model
div.p: We assume the underlying infrastructure, on which the RT-FaaS operates, is a data center topology containing multiple hosts, which altogether include m processors: π 1 , π 2 , . . . , π m . The ingress point location -through which the deployed functions are available from outside the cloud -is known beforehand. Assuming that i) the RT-FaaS platform is aware of network bandwidths and latencies within the cluster, and ii) knows the necessary execution time of real-time cloud service calls, we can form the response time matrix:

The columns represent the processors in the managed cluster, while the rows correspond to the deployments that the users want to deploy in the RT-FaaS. One cell means the response time of the deployment if its task is assigned to the considered processor. E.g., if the second deployment's function τ 2 is executed by processor π 1 , then its response time for a trigger is R 2 = r 2,1 .

In summary, a realistic input from the RT-FaaS user is a deployment request including the source code to run, its trigger period T , the used real-time cloud services, how many times they are called ω, and finally the worst case execution time c of the uploaded code without any real-time cloud service accesses. Consequently, the RT-FaaS knows a periodic task τ 1 that needs to be scheduled. From these parameters, it can calculate the execution time of τ 1 for all processors C = {C π1 , C π2 . . . , C πm }, where C πj = ω(t πj RT service )+c πj for each 1 ≤ j ≤ m. c πj is the WCET of the task (without any cloud service call) if it is run by π j processor. The task's deadline requirements can be also calculated depending on the assigned processor: D = {D π1 , D π2 . . . , D πm } where D πj = Tt i→πjt πj →i for each 1 ≤ j ≤ m. Thus, we obtained the model of the function τ 1 = (C, T, D). Then the RT-FaaS can also determine the elements of the response time matrix's row related to the deployments: r 1,j = t i→πj + C πj + t πj →i for each 1 ≤ j ≤ m. Thereby the response time of the user's deployment request relies on the set of processors: R = {r 1,1 , r 1,2 , . . . , r 1,m }. Thus, the model of the deployment is known as well: (τ 1 , R, T ). By now, one might notice that one of the main challenges of the RT-FaaS system is how to assign the requested tasks to the managed processors in order to meet their deadlines. We formalize this in Sec. IV-D.

div.head: D. ILP formalization of task partitioning
div.p: The input of the task partitioning on RT-FaaS system problem is the I = (n, m, M ) triplet, i.e., the number of tasks n and processors m, and the utilization matrix M . The utilization matrix is similar to the response-time matrix: the columns represent the processors, while rows correspond to the tasks that the user wants to run. One cell of the utilization matrix (e.g., u 1,2 ) represents the CPU utilization C π2 1 /D π2 1 of task τ 1 if it is assigned to π 2 . Our objective -see Definition 2is to find a feasible partitioning -using the least number of processors -of the given task set such that their deadline requirements are met.

The ILP formalization of the problem is the following. The two variable types are x τi πj and y πj for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and 1 ≤ j ≤ m. x τi πj denotes whether τ i is assigned to π j , while y πj indicates if any of the tasks were assigned to π j . minimize j=0...m y πj (1) subject to
div.formula: ∀τ i ∈ τ : j=1...m x τi πj = 1 (2
∀π j , j = 1...m : i=1...n C πj i D πj i × x τi πj ≤ 1 × y πj (3) ∀ j = 1 . . . m, i = 1 . . . n : x τi πj , y πj = {0, 1}(4)
div.p: The variables are x τi πj and y πj where i = 1, ..., n and j = 1, ..., m:
div.formula: x τi πj = 1, if τ i is assigned to π j 0, otherwise(5)
y πj = 1, if π j is used 0, otherwise(6)
div.p: The explanation for the constraints is the following. Each task must be assigned to exactly one host (2). The cumulative utilization of tasks assigned to the same processor must be less or equal than one due to EDF's schedulability requirement (3).

It is well known that partitioned scheduling on heterogeneous multiprocessors is intractable in polynomial time, and it is an N P-hard problem, even if processors are identical [33]. In fact, Lenstra et al. [34] have proved that no algorithm is able to find a solution in polynomial time with a smaller approximation ratio than 3/2.

div.head: E. Scheduling model
div.p: Once we know the deployment, function, and infrastructure models, the only remaining question is how to schedule the requested functions, i.e., define a scheduling model that determines where and when to execute the tasks. In this paper, we argue that one possible solution for such a system could be the partitioned EDF model, which guarantees that the tasks assigned to a particular processor are going to finish before their deadline if the sum utilization is less than one. E.g., if we assume that three tasks τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 are assigned to π 1 then it is guaranteed to meet their deadlines if
div.formula: i=τ1...τ3 C π 1 i D π 1 i ≤ 1.
div.p: This is taken care of by constraint (3) of the ILP formalization.

Consequently, the scheduling problem that we would like to solve is the following. The input includes the set of deployment requests, i.e., the deployment and function models and the infrastructure model. Applying the partitioned EDF scheduling method, we first need to partition the tasks among the processors, which is the spatial optimization part of the scheduling problem. Second, for each processor, the wellknown EDF algorithm fulfills the tasks' temporal scheduling, i.e., it decides when to start them.

div.head: V. HEURISTIC ALGORITHM FOR TASK PARTITIONING
div.p: We propose a heuristic algorithm that distributes the given task set among the processors of cluster hosts. The input of the algorithm is the same as for the ILP, i.e., the I = (n, m, M ) triplet. The steps of the proposed partitioning algorithm, denoted by ALG are the following: Step 1
Step 2

Step 3 Selecting the best processors: Given two processors π 1 and π 2 of the examined boolean matrix M . It is said that π 2 is a better processor than π 1 if and only if all 1 items in π 1 are also 1 in π 2 and w(π 2 ) > w(π 1 ). As π 2 is a better processor than π 1 , the latter is removed from the columns of M . We make this comparison for all column pairs. Definition 7. Exclusive task: Such a task that could be run by only one specific processor.

We produce the time complexity analysis of the proposed algorithm ALG to get a picture about the number of steps required in the worst-case scenario. In step 1, we sort the elements of each column of M , that takes O(mn log(n)) as any comparison sorting algorithm cannot perform better than O(n log(n)) [35]. Then, iterating through m columns and deciding for each element whether it is 1 or 0 takes O(mn) time. All in all, step 1 has O mn log(n) complexity.

Step 2 and 3 requires O(mn) iterations. Sorting the columns according to their weights takes O m log(m) . Finding the exclusive task in step 5 and iterating through its processor's column both require O(n). Finally, choosing the maximum weighted column and checking its tasks to be 1 or 0 takes again O(n) in step 6. In short, the six steps' complexity is
div.formula: O mn log(n) + O(mn) + O(mn) + O(m log(m)) + O(n) + O(n) ≈ O mn log(n) + O(m log(m)) which need to be repeated in the worst case O(m) times. Theorem 1. The time complexity of ALG is O m 2 n log(n) + log(m) .

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: To the best of our knowledge, currently, there is no publicly available real-time FaaS system, neither in academia nor in industry. Therefore, it is not possible to directly compare our proposed real-time FaaS design to another RT-FaaS scheduling approach. Instead, we focus on the evaluation of the proposed partitioning algorithm in the following.

As we have elaborated in Sec. IV, we aim to utilize the minimum number of CPUs for RT tasks -necessary to accomplish the deadline requirements -to provide the remaining ones for non-RT functions. Due to the dynamic environment of the cloud -e.g., ever-changing user loads and traffic, or frequently released cloud services delivered by the cloud provider -we argue that it is essential for realtime scheduler i) to consider a wide variety of heterogeneous processors in a multi-node cloud system, ii) to run fast (i.e., in polynomial time) to minimize scheduling overhead of the cloud nodes, and iii) not to migrate tasks among nodes. As far as we know, the most recent real-time scheduler works assume a single node environment, meaning that they either consider identical CPUs/cores [22], [23] or a limited degree of heterogeneity for the processing entities in the computing architecture. [25], [26] are good examples of the latter, they assume dual-core systems like the ARM big.LITTLE heterogeneous computing architecture that couple battery-saving and slower CPU cores (LITTLE) with more powerful and powerhungry ones (big). These schedulers are not comparable with our partitioned-EDF design since the diverse task runtimes on multiple different cores/processors cannot be modeled. That is why, in our evaluation, we use Barauh's algorithm [30] and the well-known bin-packing offline heuristic algorithm, called First Fit Decreasing (FFD) [36] as a comparison basis to our proposed approach. Baruah's approximation algorithm (BR) is based on LP-relaxation of the original ILP problem and aims to minimize the maximum fraction of the capacity of any CPU that is utilized to process RT tasks. One might notice, this objective is quite the opposite of what we aim for: BR will return a feasible partitioning that uses as many CPUs as possible to minimize the maximum cumulative utilization of the CPUs. In order to direct BR to find the minimum number of CPUs, we have extended it by wrapping it into a for a cycle. Hereinafter we refer to this extended version as EBR.

In each iteration i (from i = 0 to i = m), EBR selects the first i CPUs with the greatest weights and calls the original BR that considers only them as possible targets for the tasks. The weights are calculated as they were in the step 2 of our proposed ALG. If the original BR algorithm yields a feasible solution, then EBR breaks the for cycle and returns.

div.head: A. Simulation inputs
div.p: The simulator we have used for the comparison is opensource and available on GitHub 1 . The input for a simulation is the I = (n, m, M ) triplet, where n is the number of functions to partition, m is the number of CPUs, and M is the utilization matrix of tasks. We have used n = 10, 50, 100, 500 tasks and m = 100 CPUs. As Definition 5 specifies, in the first step ALG transforms the utilization matrix to a boolean matrix to start finding partitions. To generate a utilization matrix for the simulations, we have used this transformation inversely that works as follows. Let us assume a given a ≥ n as the number of the ones of the boolean matrix. We start with an n × m matrix of zeros. As a first step, we place a one into a randomly chosen cell of each row of the null matrix. Then we place the remaining an ones to the matrix randomly. Next, we iterate through the columns. Let us assume that the column contains b ones, we set each cell to 1 b where originally a one was placed. Then, we replace the remaining zero values with a random float number between 1 b + 0.05 and 1. Such an obtained utilization matrix guarantees that each function can be run by at least one CPU. Hereinafter instead of a we use the density feature of the boolean matrix, i.e., the percentage of non-zero (i.e, one) matrix elements. Definition 8. Density feature of the boolean matrix: a density function that returns the percentage of non-zero cells of the boolean matrix. If the density is 0% then it is a null matrix, while 100% density means an all-ones matrix.
0% density means there is no CPU on which any of the input tasks could run in real-time. The 100% density denotes all tasks could be scheduled on all CPUs.

In the following sections, we introduce how the examined partitioning algorithms perform if the number of functions and CPUs and the utilization matrix are known. Our simulations answer questions such as i) how many times the algorithms do not return a feasible solution, ii) if solutions exist, what percentage of the available CPUs are used, iii) what is the runtime complexity of the algorithms, and finally, iv) what are the answers to i and ii assuming identical multiprocessors (when the utilization values of a task's row in the utilization matrix are the same).

div.head: B. Number of feasible solutions
div.p: In Fig. 4 we depict the algorithms BR, EBR and FFD to show how many times these approaches have not returned any feasible partition solutions. ALG is not displayed since it always returned a partition in our simulations. The xaxes show the density of the boolean matrix from which the utilization matrix was generated for the simulation. We have executed one hundred simulations for a given density, each of them with different utilization matrices. The y-axes depict the percentage of simulations when the algorithms have no feasible results. In the case of BR we conclude that the more tasks are waiting for partitioning, the better the possibility 1 https://github.com/hsnlab/partitioned scheduling on RT-FaaS to find a valid partitioning. Similarly, this finding is true for EBR, furthermore, in its case, we are getting more results at a lower density value. In contrast, the FFD bin-packing heuristic algorithm provided results for a large number of tasks starting only from 7.5% density value.

div.head: C. Number of provisioned processors for RT tasks
div.p: In Fig. 5 we present how the proposed and related algorithms perform in task partitioning with the aim of minimizing the number of used CPUs for the RT functions in the partitioning result. For a given boolean matrix density, we have executed one hundred simulations with different utilization matrices. Consequently, one point in the figure represents the average number of the used CPUs of the resulted partitioning depending on the given density value. We can conclude that in general, the BR algorithm performs the weakest, regardless of the task count. This is expected, as BR's objective is the exact opposite of ours: it attempts to spread RT functions over the cluster using as many CPUs as possible. On the other hand, the EBR -that we have created to transform the original objective function to find a partitioning on the minimum number of CPUs that meets the deadlines -performs significantly better. What is more, as the input task count increases, EBR provides almost the same performance as our proposed ALG. Finally, the traditional bin-packing algorithm FFD performs between the efficient solutions (ALG,EBR) and the inefficient one (BR). Inferred from our simulations, the performance of FFD linearly decreases as the density increases, however, its success largely depends on the number of input tasks. E.g., with ten tasks, a solution is provided even for 1% density value, on the other hand, for 500 tasks, a valid solution is obtained only for > 7% density. We argue, 500 tasks in a real cloud system can be realistic, which makes FFD algorithm ineffective compared to the others.

div.head: D. Runtime complexity
div.p: Our simulations suggest that ALG and EBR are the most effective partitioning algorithms for the RT-FaaS cloud platform. Here we examine the worst-case time complexity of them. As seen in Theorem 1, the time complexity of ALG is O(m 2 (n log(n) + log(m))) ≈ O(m 2 n) (we use O from [37] to hide polylog(n) and polylog(1/δ) terms from O form).

The algorithm BR [30] includes three main steps: 1) solving the LP-relaxation of the heterogeneous multiprocessor partitioning problem, 2) determining which tasks have exactly one CPU mapping in the LP solution, and 3) for the remaining tasks constructing a bipartite graph to find exact mappings for them. Step 2 and 3 can be done in O(nm) and O(n+m) time, i.e., they are polynomial in n and m. Finding solution for a Linear Programming can be done by Interior point algorithm for which the best theoretical result -to the best of our knowledge -is O(N ω log 2 (N) log(N/δ)) ≈ O(N ω ) [38], where δ is the relative accuracy, ω is the matrix exponent, and N is the number of variables in the LP problem. In our case N = nm. This result was derandomized by Brand [37] thus providing a deterministic algorithm matches one of the fastest randomized bounds of O(N ω ). This stated bound holds for the current bound on ω with ω ≈ 2.38 [39]. So the time complexity of BR is O((nm) 2.38

For what concerns EBR, it calculates the weights of each column in the matrix -O(nm) -, sort them -O m log(m) -, and choose the first i columns -O(m) -to get the matrix M i . Then the BR algorithm is run O (nm) 2.38 . In the worst case scenario, these are repeated m times, accordingly, the overall The worst-case time complexities of the evaluated partitioning algorithms are summarized in Table I. Finally, we have investigated the scenario in which the partitioning algorithms work on a set of identical CPUs. In these simulations, the response time of deployment is independent of the CPU to which it is mapped. Consequently, in such a homogeneous utilization matrix, the values of a row are the same. We have used n = 10, 50, 100 tasks, m = 100 CPUs and generated the homogeneous utilization matrix as follows. First, we randomly selected a utilization value from a uniform distribution between 0.1 and 1 for the first task, i.e., for all the elements of the first row of the matrix. Second, we summarized the selected values so far in a variable sum and selected the next random value of a uniform distribution between 0 and min(msum, 1) for the next row. Finally, we repeated the second step for all n tasks.

div.head: E. The homogeneous multiprocessor scenario
div.p: The outcome of the simulations is illustrated in Fig. 6. The upper part, shows how many times the discussed algorithms return a feasible partitioning of the input functions. For 10 input tasks, all algorithms are able to find a solution in each simulation. Nevertheless, for 50 and 100 tasks, BR and EBR are not able to return feasible assignments for all the 100 simulations. The bottom part of the figure shows the goodness of the algorithms: the number of used CPUs in the output partitioning normalized by the task count. Inferring from the results, the input task count has no significant effect on the algorithms' performance. Furthermore, as expected, since this problem is equivalent to the Bin Packing Problem, the traditional offline heuristic algorithm FFD performs the best, followed by ALG, EBR and BR.

div.head: VII. DISCUSSION
div.p: The simulations suggest the proposed task partitioning algorithm has several advantages over the competition. ALG is the only algorithm that always found a feasible partitioning in our evaluation. Also, ALG resulted in the least number of processors for partitioning. EBR was also effective, it provided similar results as ALG for large number of tasks. However, in terms of runtime complexity, it lagged significantly behind. We also studied the case of homogeneous utilization matrices where partitioning is equivalent to the classical bin-packing problem. FFD gave the best outcome since it is designed for this problem, but ALG came in second. It produced a feasible solution for all task counts and also outperformed BR and EBR in terms of the number of provisioned CPUs for partitioning.

On the other hand, it should be mentioned that our proposed RT-FaaS scheduling model poses strong constraints both on the network and the functions. The current model does not cope with the underlying network, it simply assumes it operates in real-time. Although we believe deterministic networks will be widespread someday, currently, they are still actively researched. Furthermore, it is supposed, tasks reserve the CPUs while they are awaiting a response from external real-time cloud services, which significantly affects their execution time. We also assume that the number of calls to cloud services and the return time of them is known in advance.

In our future work, we plan to experiment with cluster scheduling where a cluster could represent the set of CPUs of a host. Within the cluster, the global RT scheduler approach could operate too, resulting in that task migration could be allowed (within a host) instead of the model presented in this paper. We also like to relax on the deterministic constraint of the network and use probabilistic or soft-real time scheduling models striving to meet task deadlines.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: There has been a growing desire to expose time-critical and computational exhaustive applications to the cloud in recent years. E.g., use-cases like remotely controlled robots or game streaming services require extremely low latency and realtime operation from the cloud platform to guarantee failurefree operation and high QoS. Our contributions are three-fold. First, we described a future RT FaaS system that could be the next step of today's cloud approaches. Second, we highlighted the missing points and the limitations of such a system and summarized the relevant related work that could be the solutions for them. Finally, we proposed a real-time scheduling method, the partitioned-EDF with our partitioning algorithm, which can execute the RT functions. Assuming heterogeneous, multi-node multiprocessor scheduling, we presented that our algorithm outperforms the related prior approaches in the number of feasible solutions, number of provisioned CPUs, and the runtime complexity.
